prompt: Based on the table, why does every state receive two more electoral votes than its House seats?

options.text: Each state adds two votes for its two U.S. senators
Each state adds two votes for its state supreme court
Each state adds two votes for its governor and lieutenant
Each state adds two votes for federal district judges

explanation: A state's electoral votes equal its House seats plus its two U.S. senators, giving even the smallest state three votes.
fun_fact: Because of the two-senator baseline, Wyoming has roughly three times more electoral votes per resident than California.

trap_notes.default: Electoral votes equal a state's House delegation plus its two U.S. senators.
trap_notes.b: State supreme courts play no role in allocating federal electoral votes.
trap_notes.c: Governors and lieutenant governors are state officials, not part of Electoral College math.
trap_notes.d: Federal judges are appointed and do not add electoral votes to a state.

prompt: What pattern in U.S. political participation does the turnout table illustrate?

options.text: Age has no measurable effect on voter turnout rates
Turnout drops in midterm elections across every age group
Younger voters participate at higher rates than older voters
Presidential elections attract fewer voters than midterms

explanation: Every age group voted at a lower rate in the 2018 midterm than in the 2020 presidential election, while older voters led both.
fun_fact: Midterm elections typically see a 15-to-25 percentage point drop in turnout compared to presidential years.

trap_notes.default: Turnout is consistently higher in presidential elections and among older age groups.
trap_notes.a: Turnout rises steadily with age in both election years shown.
trap_notes.c: The table shows 65+ voters outvoted 18–24 voters in both elections.
trap_notes.d: The 2020 presidential election drew much higher turnout than the 2018 midterm.

stimulus.title: Primary Tax Sources by Government Level

options.text: States collect most of their revenue from property taxes
The federal government relies primarily on national sales taxes
Each level of government relies primarily on a distinct tax base
Local governments depend mainly on federal payroll taxes

explanation: Federal revenue centers on income and payroll taxes, states lean on sales and income taxes, and localities rely on property taxes.
fun_fact: Property taxes fund roughly 70% of local tax collections, supporting public schools and municipal services.

trap_notes.default: Federal, state, and local governments rely on different primary tax sources.
trap_notes.a: Property taxes are the main local tax, while states rely most on sales and income taxes.
trap_notes.b: The U.S. has no national sales tax; federal revenue relies on income and payroll taxes.
trap_notes.d: Payroll taxes are a federal revenue source, not a local government tax.

stimulus.title: Sample U.S. Supreme Court Term Docket

prompt: What does the docket data demonstrate about how the U.S. Supreme Court selects cases?

options.text: The Court must hear every constitutional appeal filed by citizens
Most petitions filed with the Court receive full oral argument
The Court issues signed opinions without hearing oral arguments
The Court hears only a tiny fraction of petitions via certiorari

explanation: Using discretionary writs of certiorari and the Rule of Four, the Supreme Court selects roughly 1% of petitions for review.
fun_fact: Only four of the nine justices need to agree to grant a writ of certiorari and place a case on the docket.

trap_notes.default: The Supreme Court has broad docket discretion and hears only about 1% of petitions.
trap_notes.a: The Court is not required to hear every appeal; it grants certiorari selectively.
trap_notes.b: Only about 1.3% of filings receive oral argument.

stimulus.title: Types of Federal Grants to States

prompt: Which federal grant type gives state governments the widest discretion over how to spend federal funds?

options.text: Revenue sharing, which carries minimal federal conditions
Categorical grants, which restrict funds to narrow projects
Matching categorical grants, which require strict compliance
Project grants, which require federal agency approval

explanation: Revenue sharing places minimal conditions on states, whereas categorical grants tightly restrict how federal money is spent.
fun_fact: Congress ended general revenue sharing in 1986 due to federal deficits, leaving categorical and block grants.

trap_notes.default: Less restrictive federal conditions translate directly into higher state spending flexibility.
trap_notes.b: Categorical grants carry strict federal rules and low state flexibility.
trap_notes.c: Matching categorical grants still bind states to narrow federal rules.
trap_notes.d: Project grants are a form of categorical grant with low state discretion.

prompt: What does the legislative funnel reveal about the U.S. lawmaking process?

options.text: Over half of bills passed by one chamber become federal law
Multiple veto points eliminate most bills before enactment
Most bills introduced in Congress pass at least one chamber
Committee review guarantees a bill will reach the President

explanation: Committees, floor scheduling, bicameral passage, and presidential approval filter out over 97% of introduced bills.
fun_fact: Many bills never receive a committee hearing, which is why committees are often called legislative gatekeepers.

trap_notes.default: The constitutional lawmaking process has many hurdles, so only about 2–3% of bills become law.
trap_notes.a: Only 362 of 1,200 bills passing one chamber (about 30%) became law.
trap_notes.c: Only 8% of introduced bills even passed one chamber in the 117th Congress.
trap_notes.d: Most bills die in committee and never reach the floor or the President.

prompt: Why are congressional veto overrides so rare across all three administrations shown?

options.text: Congress may only override vetoes during a midterm year
Presidents can veto a bill again after Congress overrides it
Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers
Overriding a veto requires approval from the Supreme Court

explanation: Article I, Section 7 requires a two-thirds supermajority in both the House and Senate to override a presidential veto.
fun_fact: Historically, Congress has overridden fewer than 5% of all regular presidential vetoes.

trap_notes.default: Clearing a two-thirds supermajority in both chambers is a high constitutional bar.
trap_notes.a: Congress can override a veto in any session, not just midterm years.
trap_notes.b: Once Congress overrides a veto by two-thirds in both chambers, the bill becomes law.
trap_notes.d: The Supreme Court plays no role in the legislative veto-override process.

prompt: What relationship between education and civic participation is shown in the 2020 data?

options.text: Voters with bachelor's degrees register less often than high school graduates
Registration rates are identical across all three educational groups
High school graduates turn out at higher rates than college graduates
Higher educational attainment correlates with higher registration and turnout

explanation: Both voter registration and turnout rise steadily with formal education, reaching 80% turnout among bachelor's degree holders.
fun_fact: Political scientists link higher education with stronger civic skills and familiarity with registration rules.

trap_notes.default: Higher formal education strongly correlates with higher registration and voting rates.
trap_notes.a: Bachelor's degree holders registered at 84%, compared to 62% for high school graduates.
trap_notes.b: Registration rises by 22 percentage points across the three groups.
trap_notes.c: High school graduates turned out at 56%, lower than both college groups.

prompt: According to the table, what legal trade-off governs Super PACs compared to candidate committees?

options.text: Super PACs raise unlimited sums but may not coordinate with candidates
Super PACs face strict donor caps in exchange for direct control
Candidate committees may raise unlimited funds without disclosure
National parties are banned from coordinating with any candidates

explanation: Under Supreme Court precedent, Super PACs can raise unlimited independent funds only if they do not coordinate with candidates.
fun_fact: Super PACs must still disclose their donors publicly to the Federal Election Commission.

trap_notes.default: Independent-expenditure groups avoid contribution limits only by avoiding candidate coordination.
trap_notes.b: Candidate committees, not Super PACs, face strict donor caps and have direct control.
trap_notes.c: Candidate committees face strict per-donor contribution limits.
trap_notes.d: National parties are allowed limited coordination with their candidates.

prompt: Which statement accurately compares state legislative structures using the table?

options.text: California has more state lawmakers than New Hampshire
Nebraska is unique among the three for having a single-chamber body
Population size dictates the exact number of state lawmakers
All U.S. states require two chambers to pass state budgets

explanation: Nebraska operates the only unicameral state legislature in the U.S., while 49 states use bicameral legislatures.
fun_fact: New Hampshire's 400-member House of Representatives is the largest state legislative chamber in the country.

trap_notes.default: Nebraska is the only state with a single-chamber legislature; seat counts vary widely by state.
trap_notes.a: New Hampshire has 424 lawmakers compared to California's 120.
trap_notes.c: Small New Hampshire has 424 lawmakers, far more than populous California's 120.
trap_notes.d: Nebraska passes its state budget in a single unicameral chamber.

prompt: Why is it difficult for Congress to balance the federal budget solely by cutting annual appropriations?

options.text: Congress votes every year on Social Security benefit formulas
Net interest payments can be canceled by annual appropriations
Over 70% of spending goes to mandatory programs and debt interest
Discretionary spending accounts for nearly all federal outlays

explanation: Mandatory programs (61%) and net interest (11%) operate outside annual appropriations, leaving only 28% in discretionary bills.
fun_fact: Changing mandatory spending requires Congress to amend the underlying entitlement statutes, not just pass a budget.

trap_notes.default: Annual appropriations only cover the 28% discretionary share of federal spending.
trap_notes.a: Social Security is mandatory spending and does not require an annual vote.
trap_notes.b: The U.S. is legally obligated to pay interest on national debt to avoid default.
trap_notes.d: Discretionary spending is only 28% of total federal outlays.

prompt: What does the ratification timeline of the 27th Amendment demonstrate about Article V?

options.text: Every proposed amendment expires after seven years automatically
Ratification routinely takes longer than ten years to complete
Congress can ratify amendments without state legislative votes
Amendments without a deadline can remain pending for centuries

explanation: Because the 1789 congressional pay amendment had no time limit, states finally completed its ratification 202 years later in 1992.
fun_fact: A University of Texas student named Gregory Watson wrote a 1982 paper arguing the 1789 amendment was still alive.

trap_notes.default: Without a congressionally set deadline, proposed amendments stay open for state ratification.
trap_notes.a: Only amendments with a deadline written by Congress expire after seven years.
trap_notes.b: The 26th Amendment was ratified in just 100 days in 1971.
trap_notes.c: Article V requires three-fourths of the states to ratify every amendment.

prompt: How does proportional representation differ from single-member plurality in the table?

options.text: It aligns a party's legislative seat share with its vote share
It automatically gives a 35% party an outright legislative majority
It eliminates minor parties from winning any legislative seats
It awards bonus seats to the party finishing in first place

explanation: Proportional representation translates 35% of the vote into 35% of seats, whereas single-member plurality can yield a majority.
fun_fact: Because proportional systems rarely give one party 50% alone, they usually produce coalition governments.

trap_notes.default: Proportional representation matches seat shares closely to national vote percentages.
trap_notes.b: In the table, only single-member plurality gave Party A a 52-seat majority.
trap_notes.c: Proportional representation actually helps smaller parties win seats.
trap_notes.d: Single-member plurality, not proportional representation, magnified Party A's seat count.

prompt: How does the council-manager form separate political leadership from daily administration?

options.text: State governors appoint city managers to oversee local budgets
An elected council hires a professional manager to run city operations
An elected mayor appoints both the council and department heads
Voters directly elect every municipal department administrator

explanation: In council-manager cities, the elected council sets policy and hires a nonpartisan professional city manager to administer services.
fun_fact: Council-manager government is the most common form in mid-sized U.S. cities, including Phoenix and San Antonio.

trap_notes.default: Council-manager systems pair an elected council with an appointed professional city manager.
trap_notes.a: Local city councils, not state governors, hire the city manager.
trap_notes.c: Voters, not mayors, elect city councils.
trap_notes.d: In a council-manager system, the council appoints the city manager.

prompt: Why did New York lose 15 House seats while Texas and Florida gained 31 combined between 1960 and 2020?

options.text: New York voluntarily surrendered seats to lower its federal taxes
States with larger land area automatically receive extra House seats
The 435 House seats are reapportioned as population shifts southward
Congress expanded the House past 435 seats to reward Sun Belt states

explanation: Because the House is capped at 435 seats, faster population growth in Sun Belt states shifts seats away from slower-growing states.
fun_fact: The Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929 fixed the size of the U.S. House of Representatives at 435 seats.

trap_notes.default: House seats are fixed at 435, so regional population shifts reallocate seats after each census.
trap_notes.a: States cannot trade or surrender House seats; apportionment is constitutional.
trap_notes.b: House seats are apportioned by population, not geographic land area.
trap_notes.d: The House has remained capped at 435 voting seats since 1929.

prompt: Where does a federal criminal or civil lawsuit normally begin in the federal court system?

options.text: In one of the 13 U.S. Courts of Appeals
Directly in the U.S. Supreme Court
In a state appellate court first
In one of the 94 U.S. District Courts

explanation: U.S. District Courts are the general trial courts of the federal system, where evidence is presented and juries sit.
fun_fact: Every U.S. state has at least one federal judicial district, and larger states like California and Texas have four.

trap_notes.default: Federal trials begin in U.S. District Courts before any appeal to Circuit Courts.
trap_notes.a: Courts of Appeals review District Court decisions; they do not hold original trials.
trap_notes.b: The Supreme Court rarely exercises original jurisdiction, mostly hearing appeals.
trap_notes.c: Federal cases start in federal District Courts, not state appellate courts.

prompt: What unique general-election outcome can a top-two primary produce compared to open or closed primaries?

options.text: Two candidates from the same party can face each other
Independent voters are barred from casting a primary ballot
Every political party is guaranteed a spot on the November ballot
Only registered party members determine the two finalists

explanation: Because the top two vote-getters advance regardless of party, two candidates from the same party can meet in November.
fun_fact: California and Washington both use top-two primaries for congressional and statewide offices.

trap_notes.default: Top-two primaries advance the highest two finishers regardless of party label.
trap_notes.b: Any registered voter, including independents, can vote in a top-two primary.
trap_notes.c: Parties that finish third or lower do not advance to the general election.
trap_notes.d: Closed primaries, not top-two primaries, restrict voting to party members.

prompt: Which trend across all three branches of the U.S. government is shown in the polling table?

Public trust in Congress rose above trust in the Supreme Court
The executive branch maintained majority public trust in 2023

explanation: Trust fell in all three branches between 2000 and 2023, with Congress dropping 34 points to the lowest level at 34%.
fun_fact: Despite falling from 75% to 47%, the judicial branch remained the most trusted of the three branches.

trap_notes.default: All three branches saw major trust declines, with Congress dropping the most (34 points).
trap_notes.a: Congress dropped 34 points (68% to 34%), while the judicial branch dropped 28 points.
trap_notes.c: Congress fell to 34% in 2023, remaining below the judicial branch at 47%.
trap_notes.d: Executive trust fell to 41% in 2023, below a 50% majority.

prompt: What does the variation in state tax mixes illustrate about U.S. federalism?

options.text: Congress sets uniform state sales tax rates across the nation
States without sales taxes cannot fund public infrastructure
States retain broad authority to design distinct tax systems
The U.S. Constitution requires every state to levy an income tax

explanation: Under federalism, states choose their own tax mixes—Oregon relies on income taxes without sales tax, while Texas does the reverse.
fun_fact: Nine U.S. states levy no broad individual income tax, while five levy no statewide general sales tax.

trap_notes.default: Federalism allows each state to choose its own combination of income, sales, and other taxes.
trap_notes.a: States set their own sales tax rates; Oregon chooses a 0% statewide sales tax.
trap_notes.b: Oregon funds state infrastructure using its income tax and other revenues.
trap_notes.d: Texas levies 0% individual income tax, showing it is not constitutionally required.

prompt: What shift in U.S. Senate governance is reflected in the cloture data?

options.text: Senators stopped using cloture motions after the 1970s
Cloture motions were easier to defeat in 2022 than in 1970
The House of Representatives adopted Senate cloture rules in 2021
Filibuster threats and cloture votes became routine legislative hurdles

trap_notes.default: Cloture filings skyrocketed over five decades as filibuster threats became routine.
trap_notes.a: Cloture filings increased nearly fiftyfold after 1970.
trap_notes.b: In 2021–2022, 270 of 328 cloture motions succeeded, compared to 0 of 7 in 1969–1970.

prompt: Which constitutional power authorizes Congress to set the uniform naturalization rules reflected in the table?

Article III power granting federal courts control of immigration visas

trap_notes.b: States do not grant U.S. citizenship; naturalization is an enumerated federal power.
trap_notes.c: The Third Amendment deals with quartering soldiers, not citizenship.
trap_notes.d: Article III covers federal judicial power, not naturalization rules.

prompt: What pattern in direct democracy does the ballot measure table highlight?

options.text: Veto referendums are proposed by governors rather than voters
Measures placed on the ballot by legislatures pass more often than citizen initiatives
Citizen initiatives pass at a higher rate than legislative referrals

trap_notes.c: Citizen initiatives passed at 44%, well below legislative referrals at 74%.

prompt: How does the veto power of permanent UN Security Council members shape international action?

options.text: The United Kingdom used its veto more often after 1992 than before
Only the United States and Russia hold veto power on the Council

trap_notes.a: The UK cast 0 vetoes between 1992 and 2023, down from 30 during the Cold War.
trap_notes.b: China and France also hold permanent seats and veto power.
trap_notes.d: Rotating members cannot override a permanent member's veto.

stimulus.title: U.S. Public K–12 School Funding Shares

prompt: Why do interest groups lobby both Congress and executive agencies like HHS or the FTC?

Executive agencies have sole power to pass federal tax laws

Executive agencies appoint U.S. senators to oversight committees

prompt: Why did Franklin Roosevelt issue far more executive orders per year than modern presidents in the table?

The Great Depression and World War II prompted sweeping executive action
The 22nd Amendment required modern presidents to issue fewer orders
Congress lacked authority to pass laws during the 1930s and 1940s

prompt: What does the federal criminal data show about how the Sixth Amendment right to a trial operates in practice?

The Sixth Amendment forbids defendants from entering guilty pleas

Nearly all federal criminal cases are decided by a twelve-person jury

trap_notes.a: Only 8% of federal criminal cases are dismissed.
trap_notes.b: Defendants may voluntarily waive their right to a jury trial and plead guilty.
trap_notes.d: Only 2% of federal criminal cases go to trial.

prompt: How does the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) support democratic accountability in the United States?

It requires private corporations to publish all trade secrets
It abolishes all national security classification rules
It lets citizens and journalists request executive-branch records

fun_fact: FOIA includes nine exemptions protecting classified defense data, personal privacy, and trade secrets.

trap_notes.a: FOIA applies to federal executive agencies, not the judicial branch or jury rooms.
trap_notes.b: FOIA covers federal government agencies, not private corporate records.

prompt: Based on the table, how are electoral systems linked to women's legislative representation?

The United States has a higher share of women lawmakers than Sweden

trap_notes.c: The U.S. sits at 29%, lower than both the UK (35%) and Sweden (46%).

prompt: What major shift in U.S. election administration occurred between 2016 and 2020?

More than two-thirds of voters cast ballots before Election Day in 2020
Mail voting declined sharply between 2016 and 2020
States eliminated early in-person voting during 2020

prompt: How did Chief Justice John Marshall establish judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803)?

options.text: He amended Article III to create lower federal district courts
He ruled that state legislatures could nullify federal statutes
He struck down part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 as unconstitutional
He ordered President Jefferson to appoint all Federalist judges

trap_notes.a: Courts cannot amend the Constitution; Article V governs constitutional amendments.
trap_notes.b: Marshall's Court later rejected state nullification in cases like McCulloch v. Maryland.

prompt: How did Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) reshape both U.S. federalism and the national economy?

options.text: It allowed states to tax goods crossing state borders without limit
It barred the federal government from regulating waterways or railroads
It protected New York's steamboat monopoly under the Tenth Amendment
It gave Congress broad authority over interstate commerce, ending state monopolies

fun_fact: Breaking up state-granted monopolies lowered steamboat fares and spurred a national market.

trap_notes.default: Gibbons v. Ogden interpreted Congress's Commerce Clause power broadly to foster an integrated market.
trap_notes.a: The Constitution's Import-Export and Commerce Clauses bar states from erecting interstate tariffs.
trap_notes.b: The ruling confirmed, rather than barred, federal authority over interstate waterways.
trap_notes.c: The Court struck down New York's monopoly because it conflicted with a federal coasting license.

prompt: Which idea from Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) directly shaped Articles I–III of the U.S. Constitution?

options.text: Dividing legislative, executive, and judicial power prevents tyranny
Absolute monarchy provides the most stable protection for liberty

trap_notes.b: Montesquieu critiqued absolute monarchy as prone to despotism.
trap_notes.c: Concentrating all power in one assembly violates separation of powers.
trap_notes.d: Montesquieu believed pure direct democracy suited small city-states, not vast republics.

prompt: How has postwar internal migration to the Sun Belt altered national representation in Washington, D.C.?

It shifted House seats and electors from the Frost Belt to the Sun Belt
It increased the number of U.S. senators representing Sun Belt states
It reduced the total number of voting House members below 435 seats

trap_notes.a: The Constitution mandates a decennial census specifically to reapportion seats.
trap_notes.c: Every state receives exactly two U.S. senators regardless of population.

prompt: Why was Gitlow v. New York (1925) a turning point in applying the Bill of Rights to the states?

options.text: It repealed the First Amendment's protection of political speech
It allowed state governors to suspend the 14th Amendment in wartime
It used the 14th Amendment Due Process Clause to apply free speech to states
It ruled that the Bill of Rights restricts only the federal government

trap_notes.a: The Supreme Court cannot repeal constitutional amendments.
trap_notes.b: State governors have no authority to suspend federal constitutional amendments.
trap_notes.d: Barron v. Baltimore (1833) held that rule before the 14th Amendment; Gitlow reversed that trend.

prompt: How did McCulloch v. Maryland (1819) support federal economic institutions against state interference?

options.text: It ruled that only state-chartered banks could issue paper currency
It allowed Maryland to tax federal institutions at 10 percent
It abolished the Second Bank of the United States as unconstitutional
It affirmed implied power to charter a national bank and barred state taxes on it

explanation: Marshall invoked the Necessary and Proper Clause for the bank and the Supremacy Clause to block Maryland's tax.
fun_fact: The ruling protected federal agencies from hostile state taxation across the growing republic.

trap_notes.default: McCulloch upheld implied congressional power and federal supremacy over state taxation.
trap_notes.a: The Court upheld Congress's power to charter a national bank.
trap_notes.b: The Court struck down Maryland's tax under the Supremacy Clause.
trap_notes.c: President Andrew Jackson later vetoed the bank's recharter in 1832, not the Court in 1819.

prompt: How did John Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) influence the Declaration of Independence?

options.text: It argued that governments derive legitimacy from consent to protect natural rights
It defended the divine right of kings against parliamentary rebellion
It proposed abolishing private property in favor of communal ownership
It urged colonies to remain loyal to monarchs regardless of grievances

explanation: Jefferson echoed Locke's social contract: people have natural rights, and when government violates them, citizens may alter or abolish it.
fun_fact: Locke listed natural rights as 'life, liberty, and estate,' which Jefferson adapted to 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.'

trap_notes.default: Locke's social contract and natural-rights philosophy underpin the Declaration's justification for independence.
trap_notes.b: Locke wrote his First Treatise specifically to refute the divine right of kings.
trap_notes.c: Locke strongly defended individual property rights as a core natural right.
trap_notes.d: Locke argued citizens have a right to revolt against tyrannical rulers.

prompt: How do 'packing' and 'cracking' manipulate spatial geography during legislative redistricting?

options.text: They assign extra U.S. senators to densely populated urban areas
They concentrate rival voters in few districts or split them across many
They require every legislative district to follow county boundaries
They ensure every district has an identical geographic land area

explanation: Packing wastes rival votes in landslide districts, while cracking dilutes rival majorities across several neighboring districts.
fun_fact: In Rucho v. Common Cause (2019), the Supreme Court held federal courts cannot police purely partisan gerrymanders.

trap_notes.default: Partisan mapmakers use geographic packing and cracking to maximize wasted opposition votes.
trap_notes.a: U.S. senators represent entire states, not redrawn geographic districts.
trap_notes.c: Gerrymandered maps frequently slice across county and city lines.
trap_notes.d: Districts must have roughly equal populations, not equal land areas.

prompt: Why was the Voting Rights Act of 1965 needed nearly a century after the 15th Amendment?

options.text: Women were still barred from voting nationwide until 1965
The Supreme Court had repealed the 15th Amendment in 1954
Literacy tests and intimidation still blocked Black citizens from voting
The 15th Amendment applied only to presidential elections, not local ones

explanation: State literacy tests, poll taxes, and intimidation nullified 15th Amendment rights until federal law banned those barriers in 1965.
fun_fact: Within four years of the 1965 act, Black voter registration in Mississippi jumped from under 7% to nearly 60%.

trap_notes.default: Jim Crow barriers persisted until federal enforcement under the 1965 Voting Rights Act.
trap_notes.a: The 19th Amendment guaranteed women's suffrage nationwide in 1920.
trap_notes.b: The Supreme Court cannot repeal constitutional amendments.
trap_notes.d: The 15th Amendment covered all elections, but states evaded it with discriminatory tests.

prompt: How did the 16th Amendment (1913) change federal fiscal capacity?

options.text: It banned the federal government from collecting tariffs on imported goods
It required states to turn over local property taxes to the Treasury
It capped federal income tax rates at a flat two percent
It empowered Congress to levy a federal income tax without state apportionment

explanation: The 16th Amendment overturned Pollock v. Farmers' Loan & Trust Co., letting Congress enact a progressive income tax.
fun_fact: Before 1913, tariffs and excise taxes provided the bulk of federal government revenue.

trap_notes.default: The 16th Amendment authorized unapportioned federal income taxes, shifting revenue away from tariffs.
trap_notes.a: Tariffs remained legal under Article I, Section 8.
trap_notes.b: Local property taxes stay with local and state governments.
trap_notes.c: The 16th Amendment set no cap on income tax rates.

prompt: Which principle from Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) is echoed in the Fifth Amendment Due Process Clause?

options.text: No free person may be imprisoned or stripped of property without lawful judgment
Every citizen has the right to vote directly on national tax rates
Monarchs hold absolute immunity from parliamentary oversight
Religious minorities must be granted separate legislative chambers

explanation: Magna Carta's guarantee against arbitrary arrest without 'the law of the land' evolved into American constitutional due process.
fun_fact: English jurist Edward Coke helped popularize 'due process of law' as the modern translation of 'law of the land.'

trap_notes.default: Magna Carta planted the rule-of-law seed that grew into the Fifth Amendment's Due Process Clause.
trap_notes.b: Magna Carta was a baronial charter, not a system of universal voting.
trap_notes.c: Magna Carta limited, rather than expanded, royal immunity.
trap_notes.d: Magna Carta did not establish separate religious legislative chambers.

prompt: Why do presidential campaigns concentrate visits and ads in a handful of battleground states?

options.text: Electoral votes in safe states are divided proportionally by county
Winner-take-all state rules award all electors even for a narrow plurality
The Constitution bans campaigning in states with large populations
Only battleground states are permitted to hold presidential primaries

explanation: Because 48 states use winner-take-all rules, winning a safe state by more votes adds zero extra electors, focusing focus on swing states.
fun_fact: Maine and Nebraska are the only two states that allocate some electoral votes by congressional district.

trap_notes.default: Winner-take-all state allocation makes closely divided swing states decisive for reaching 270.
trap_notes.a: No state allocates electoral votes by county.
trap_notes.c: Candidates can campaign in any state; strategy, not law, drives swing-state focus.
trap_notes.d: Every state holds presidential primaries or caucuses.

prompt: Why did Congress pass the War Powers Resolution of 1973 over President Nixon's veto?

options.text: To abolish the President's constitutional role as Commander in Chief
To require United Nations approval before any U.S. military deployment
To reassert legislative checks after undeclared executive wars in Vietnam
To transfer the power to declare war from Congress to the Pentagon

explanation: After Vietnam, Congress required presidents to report troop deployments within 48 hours and seek approval within 60 days.
fun_fact: Every president since 1973 has questioned the War Powers Resolution's constitutionality, though most submit reports.

trap_notes.default: The 1973 War Powers Resolution aimed to curb unilateral presidential troop commitments after Vietnam.
trap_notes.a: Statutes cannot abolish the President's Article II Commander-in-Chief role.
trap_notes.b: The law requires congressional authorization, not UN permission.
trap_notes.d: Congress sought to reclaim, not surrender, war-making oversight.

prompt: Why did Congress structure the Federal Reserve Board with 14-year staggered terms?

options.text: To allow the President to fire governors over interest-rate disagreements
To give private commercial banks control over federal income tax rates
To place the central bank outside all congressional statutory authority
To insulate monetary policy from short-term electoral pressure

explanation: Long, staggered terms prevent a single president from packing the Board, helping the Fed fight inflation even before elections.
fun_fact: The Federal Reserve Chair still testifies twice a year before Congress to maintain democratic accountability.

trap_notes.default: Staggered 14-year terms shield monetary policy from short-term political pressure to print money.
trap_notes.a: Fed governors can only be removed 'for cause,' not over policy disagreements.
trap_notes.b: Congress, not private banks, sets federal income tax rates.
trap_notes.c: Congress created the Fed by statute and can amend its mandate at any time.

prompt: According to Duverger's Law, why does the U.S. have two major parties while the Netherlands has many?

options.text: Single-member plurality districts favor two parties, while proportional lists aid many
The U.S. Constitution bans third parties from appearing on federal ballots
Dutch law requires every citizen to join at least two political parties
Parliamentary systems typically produce fewer parties than presidential ones

explanation: Single-member districts penalize minor parties under Duverger's Law, whereas proportional lists let small parties win seats.
fun_fact: In the Netherlands, a party needs less than 1% of the national vote to win a seat in the 150-member lower house.

trap_notes.default: Electoral rules shape party systems: plurality districts produce two-party competition, while PR yields multiparty systems.
trap_notes.b: Third parties regularly appear on U.S. ballots, though winner-take-all rules limit their wins.
trap_notes.c: Dutch citizens are not required to join political parties.
trap_notes.d: Proportional parliamentary systems typically produce more parties, not fewer.

prompt: How does the Constitution's Compact Clause help seven western states manage the Colorado River?

options.text: It forbids states from cooperating on shared environmental resources
It lets states form binding regional water agreements with congressional consent
It lets upstream states divert all river water without consulting neighbors
It transfers all state river ownership directly to county sheriffs

explanation: Under Article I, Section 10, states negotiated the 1922 Colorado River Compact, approved by Congress, to divide water shares.
fun_fact: Over 200 interstate compacts operate in the U.S. today, covering bridges, transit, and river basins.

trap_notes.default: Article I, Section 10 allows interstate compacts with congressional consent to solve cross-border problems.
trap_notes.a: The Compact Clause enables, rather than forbids, interstate cooperation.
trap_notes.c: The Supreme Court settles interstate water disputes equitably rather than allowing total upstream diversion.
trap_notes.d: Interstate compacts are state-level agreements approved by Congress, not county sheriffs.

prompt: What constitutional test did Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes announce in Schenck v. United States (1919) during World War I?

options.text: Congress may outlaw all criticism of the President during peacetime
Newspapers must submit every wartime article for prior censorship
Speech creating a 'clear and present danger' may be restricted by Congress
Anti-draft leaflets are protected even if they spark immediate mutiny

explanation: Holmes upheld Charles Schenck's Espionage Act conviction, ruling wartime speech creating a clear and present danger is not absolute.
fun_fact: Fifty years later, Brandenburg v. Ohio (1969) replaced Holmes's test with a stricter 'imminent lawless action' standard.

trap_notes.default: Schenck established that wartime emergencies can narrow First Amendment speech protections.
trap_notes.a: Schenck focused on wartime draft obstruction, not peacetime criticism of the President.
trap_notes.b: Near v. Minnesota (1931) strongly barred prior restraint of the press.
trap_notes.d: The Court upheld Schenck's conviction for distributing anti-draft leaflets.

prompt: Why do state governors generally prefer federal block grants over categorical grants?

options.text: Block grants require no reporting or auditing by state agencies
Categorical grants force states to cut all state-level taxes
Block grants are repaid to the federal Treasury with interest
Block grants let states tailor funds to local economic priorities

explanation: Block grants bundle funds for broad goals like community development, giving states flexibility instead of rigid federal mandates.
fun_fact: The 1996 welfare reform replaced a categorical entitlement with the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) block grant.

trap_notes.default: Block grants reduce federal strings, letting states allocate resources where local needs are greatest.
trap_notes.a: Block grants still require basic auditing and compliance with broad statutory goals.
trap_notes.b: Categorical grants do not force states to cut their own taxes.
trap_notes.c: Grants-in-aid are federal transfers, not loans repaid with interest.

prompt: Which protection in the U.S. Eighth Amendment was borrowed almost word-for-word from the English Bill of Rights (1689)?

options.text: Bans on excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments
Guarantees of universal public education for all children
Separation of church and state through the Establishment Clause
Creation of an independent federal central bank

explanation: Both the 1689 English Bill of Rights and the 1791 Eighth Amendment prohibit excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel punishments.
fun_fact: The English Bill of Rights was drafted after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 to curb royal abuses.

trap_notes.default: The Eighth Amendment's ban on excessive bail and cruel punishments traces directly to 1689 England.
trap_notes.b: Public education is not mentioned in either the English Bill of Rights or the Eighth Amendment.
trap_notes.c: England kept an established church (Church of England) in 1689.
trap_notes.d: Central banking is unrelated to the Eighth Amendment.

prompt: How does the Great Compromise's equal Senate rule affect rural versus urban representation today?

options.text: Rural states have no voting representation in the House of Representatives
Less populous rural states hold disproportionately greater per-capita Senate power
More populous urban states receive extra senators after each census
Every U.S. city with over one million residents elects its own senator

explanation: Giving Wyoming (~580,000 people) and California (~39 million) two senators each amplifies rural states' per-capita Senate influence.
fun_fact: Article V makes equal state suffrage in the Senate the only constitutional clause that cannot be amended without a state's consent.

trap_notes.default: Equal Senate representation gives small-population rural states greater per-capita voting weight.
trap_notes.a: Every state is guaranteed at least one voting representative in the House.
trap_notes.c: Every state gets two senators regardless of population.
trap_notes.d: Cities do not elect their own U.S. senators.

prompt: How did western states like Wyoming and Colorado build momentum toward the 19th Amendment (1920)?

options.text: The Supreme Court banned state-level women's suffrage before 1920
Southern states adopted women's suffrage before any western territory
State-level suffrage wins proved women voters could shape federal politics
Western states seceded from Congress until women's suffrage passed

explanation: By 1918, over a dozen mostly western states had granted women full suffrage, pressuring Congress and the states to pass the 19th Amendment.
fun_fact: Montana's Jeannette Rankin became the first woman elected to Congress in 1916—four years before the 19th Amendment.

trap_notes.default: State-by-state suffrage victories in the West created political leverage for a national amendment.
trap_notes.a: The Supreme Court never banned states from granting women the right to vote.
trap_notes.b: Western territories and states led the nation in adopting women's suffrage.
trap_notes.d: Western states worked within Congress rather than seceding.

prompt: What economic and political change followed Citizens United v. FEC (2010)?

options.text: Corporations were permitted to donate unlimited cash directly to candidates
Congress banned all political advertising within sixty days of elections
The Federal Election Commission was dissolved as unconstitutional
Corporations and unions gained First Amendment rights to spend unlimited independent funds

explanation: Citizens United struck down limits on independent corporate and union political spending, fueling the rise of Super PACs.
fun_fact: The ruling kept federal bans on direct corporate donations to candidate campaigns intact.

trap_notes.default: Citizens United lifted bans on independent corporate/union expenditures, not direct candidate donations.
trap_notes.a: Direct corporate contributions to federal candidates remain illegal.
trap_notes.b: Citizens United actually struck down the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act's blackout period.
trap_notes.c: The FEC remains the federal agency enforcing campaign disclosure and contribution rules.

prompt: How did the Roman Republic's mixed constitution inspire the framers of the U.S. Constitution?

options.text: It balanced executive consuls, an aristocratic Senate, and popular assemblies
It relied on hereditary emperors to appoint all judges for life
It eliminated written laws so leaders could rule by oral decree
It banned citizens from serving in elected assemblies

explanation: The framers admired Rome's balanced republic—mixing executive authority, a deliberative Senate, and popular assemblies—to check tyranny.
fun_fact: The U.S. Senate and the Latin word 'capitol' both take their names directly from ancient Roman institutions.

trap_notes.default: Rome's mixed republic modeled checks and balances among executive, deliberative, and popular institutions.
trap_notes.b: Hereditary emperors replaced the Roman Republic later; the framers admired the Republic.
trap_notes.c: Rome codified the Twelve Tables so laws would be public and written.
trap_notes.d: Roman citizens voted in popular assemblies to pass laws and elect magistrates.

prompt: How does the political status of U.S. territories like Puerto Rico and Guam differ from U.S. states?

options.text: Territories are legally exempt from all federal statutes
Residents are U.S. citizens but lack voting senators and Electoral College votes
Residents are barred from serving in the U.S. armed forces
Each territory elects two voting U.S. senators to Congress

explanation: Under Article IV's Territory Clause, territories elect non-voting House delegates and do not cast Electoral College votes.
fun_fact: Residents of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands can vote in presidential primaries even without general-election electors.

trap_notes.default: U.S. territories have non-voting House delegates and no U.S. senators or presidential electors.
trap_notes.a: Congress holds broad legislative authority over U.S. territories under Article IV.
trap_notes.c: Residents of U.S. territories serve in the U.S. military at high rates.
trap_notes.d: Only U.S. states elect voting U.S. senators.

prompt: What constitutional tension did Korematsu v. United States (1944) expose during World War II?

options.text: State governors refused to enforce the 19th Amendment during wartime
The Supreme Court struck down Executive Order 9066 in 1944
Executive wartime security claims clashed with Fifth Amendment equal protection
Congress attempted to impeach President Roosevelt over tariff policy

explanation: The Court upheld Japanese American internment under wartime deference in 1944, a ruling later repudiated in 2018.
fun_fact: Congress formally apologized and paid reparations to surviving internees through the Civil Liberties Act of 1988.

trap_notes.default: Korematsu highlighted how wartime executive power can threaten minority civil liberties.
trap_notes.a: The case involved federal military exclusion orders, not the 19th Amendment.
trap_notes.b: The 1944 Court upheld the exclusion order; it did not strike it down.
trap_notes.d: Korematsu concerned Executive Order 9066 and internment, not tariff impeachment.

prompt: How do federal agencies like the EPA and FTC regulate the U.S. economy within constitutional limits?

options.text: They pass their own federal tax laws without congressional approval
They operate without judicial review by federal courts
They replace state legislatures on all local zoning matters
They issue binding rules under authority delegated by congressional statutes

explanation: Congress delegates technical rulemaking to expert agencies, whose regulations carry force of law under the Administrative Procedure Act.
fun_fact: Federal agencies must publish proposed rules in the Federal Register and invite public comments before finalizing them.

trap_notes.default: Regulatory agencies exercise delegated statutory authority, subject to public notice and court review.
trap_notes.a: Only Congress can enact federal taxes.
trap_notes.b: Federal courts regularly review agency rules to ensure they stay within statutory bounds.
trap_notes.c: Local zoning remains a municipal and state responsibility.

prompt: How does removing a British prime minister via no-confidence differ from U.S. presidential impeachment?

options.text: No-confidence removes a prime minister over politics; impeachment requires high crimes
Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House to remove a president
British prime ministers serve fixed four-year terms immune from Parliament
U.S. presidents are removed automatically if their party loses the House

explanation: A parliamentary majority can oust a prime minister over politics, whereas U.S. impeachment requires conviction for serious offenses.
fun_fact: No U.S. president has ever been removed from office by a Senate impeachment conviction.

trap_notes.default: Parliamentary no-confidence is a political tool; U.S. impeachment is a constitutional trial for misconduct.
trap_notes.b: The House impeaches by majority, but removal requires a two-thirds Senate conviction.
trap_notes.c: Prime ministers depend on Parliament's confidence and can be replaced mid-term.
trap_notes.d: Divided government is common in the U.S.; losing Congress does not remove the President.

prompt: What rights does a coastal state hold within its 200-nautical-mile Exclusive Economic Zone under UNCLOS?

options.text: Ownership of all international waters across the entire ocean
Sovereign rights over fishing and seabed resources, while allowing foreign navigation
Total ban on all foreign commercial ships passing through the zone
Control over all airspace and territory of neighboring island nations

explanation: The 1982 Law of the Sea treaty grants coastal states resource rights out to 200 nautical miles while keeping navigation free.
fun_fact: Full territorial sovereignty extends only 12 nautical miles from a state's coastline.

trap_notes.default: EEZs grant resource rights out to 200 nautical miles without blocking peaceful foreign shipping.
trap_notes.a: Waters beyond 200 nautical miles are the high seas, open to all nations.
trap_notes.c: Freedom of navigation for foreign ships is protected inside an EEZ.
trap_notes.d: An EEZ covers maritime resources, not the land or airspace of other nations.

prompt: How did Baker v. Carr (1962) and subsequent rulings reshape legislative representation in the states?

options.text: They gave rural counties permanent extra seats regardless of population
They abolished state senates across the United States
They allowed federal courts to enforce 'one person, one vote' equal districts
They ruled that state legislative maps are immune from Equal Protection review

explanation: Baker v. Carr made malapportionment justiciable under the 14th Amendment, leading to equal-population districts.
fun_fact: Before 1962, Tennessee had not redrawn its legislative districts since 1901 despite massive urban growth.

trap_notes.default: Baker v. Carr opened the door for federal courts to require equal-population legislative districts.
trap_notes.a: Reynolds v. Sims (1964) struck down county-based state senate maps that ignored population.
trap_notes.b: States kept their bicameral senates, but had to draw them by equal population.
trap_notes.d: The Court rejected the claim that malapportionment was a non-justiciable political question.

prompt: What two constitutional conditions must government meet when exercising eminent domain under the Fifth Amendment?

options.text: The owner must consent in writing and receive a tax exemption
Only state governors may take land, without paying market value
Congress must pass a constitutional amendment for each parcel taken
The taking must serve a public use and provide just compensation

explanation: The Fifth Amendment Takings Clause balances infrastructure needs with property rights by requiring public use and fair compensation.
fun_fact: In Kelo v. City of New London (2005), the Court ruled economic development can qualify as 'public use,' prompting state limits.

trap_notes.default: Eminent domain allows government property takings only for public use and with just compensation.
trap_notes.a: Eminent domain does not require the property owner's consent.
trap_notes.b: Federal, state, and local governments may use eminent domain, always with just compensation.
trap_notes.c: No constitutional amendment is needed; courts oversee public use and fair market value.
